title: Headings, Paragraphs, and Text
description: Use heading levels to express document hierarchy, use paragraphs for ordinary text, and recognize/correct common heading mistakes.

objectives.statement: Explain why heading levels should reflect document hierarchy rather than desired visual size.
Identify and correct common heading-structure mistakes, such as skipped levels or choosing a heading for its visual size.
Build a short HTML document with a logical heading hierarchy and ordinary paragraphs.

content.title: Headings, Paragraphs, and Text
content.hook: A page with six h1 tags because 'they're all important' isn't well-structured — it's an outline with no outline.
content.context: Headings are one of the places beginners most often confuse 'what it means' with 'how it looks.'
goals: Choose heading levels for meaning, not size
Build a document with a logical hierarchy

content.title: Headings Are an Outline, Not a Font Picker
content.text: Heading elements h1 through h6 express the logical structure of a document — h1 is the top-level heading, h2 is a major section within it, h3 a subsection of that, and so on. This hierarchy matters to more than just readers: screen readers let users jump between headings the way you might use a table of contents, and that only works if the levels reflect real structure. A heading level should never be chosen because 'it looks the right size' — if a heading looks wrong, that's fixed with CSS, not by picking a different, structurally incorrect heading level. Ordinary blocks of text — the actual content, not titles — belong in paragraph elements.

callout.text: Skipping straight from h1 to h4 to get a smaller-looking heading breaks the outline for anyone relying on heading structure to navigate.

content.keyTakeaway: Choose a heading level for what it means in the outline, not for how large it currently renders.

content.question: A page's main title is marked up with h1. Below it, three major sections each need their own heading. What level should those section headings be?

options.text: h2, since they're a level below the page's main h1
h4, to make them look appropriately smaller
It doesn't matter as long as they're bold

content.explanation: Major sections directly under the page's h1 belong one level down, at h2, regardless of how large or small they should look.

feedback.correct: Right — one level below the page's h1 is h2.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite — think about what level comes directly below h1 in the outline, not about visual size.

content.title: Fix the Broken Heading Hierarchy
content.prompt: This page's headings were chosen for how they look, not what they mean. Find the structural mistake and fix it.
content.buggyCode:

content.bugDescription: The article's own title uses h4, jumping past h2 and h3, apparently because h4 looked like the right size — while the unrelated 'Related Posts' section correctly uses h2.
fixRequirements: The article title should be h2, directly below the page's h1
No heading level should be skipped
content.solutionCode:

hints: Compare the article title's heading level to the 'Related Posts' heading level — they should be structural equals.
Which level comes directly below h1?

feedback.correct: Right — the article title is a top-level section just like 'Related Posts', so it should be the same level.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at what level 'Related Posts' uses — the article title is structurally the same kind of section.

content.title: Build a Short Document with a Logical Hierarchy
content.prompt: Build a short HTML document about your favorite hobby with one h1 page title, two h2 section headings below it, and a paragraph of text under each section heading.
content.instructions: Use exactly one h1, two h2 elements, and a p under each h2.
content.solutionCode:
Rock Climbing

Getting Started

Most climbers begin at an indoor bouldering gym...

Gear

Climbing shoes and chalk are the essentials to start...

feedback.correct: That's a document with a clean, logical heading hierarchy.
feedback.incorrect: Check the count of h1/h2 elements and make sure each section has a paragraph beneath it.

content.title: What You Should Take Away
takeaways: Heading levels express document structure, not desired visual size.
Skipping heading levels breaks the outline for readers and assistive technology alike.
Ordinary text belongs in paragraphs; headings are for structural section titles.
